title: Apple App Store search snapshot: mystery/detective/puzzle queries in six Arab storefronts (SA, AE, EG, KW, JO, MA), 2026-10-27
authors: ATHAR W2-AUDIENCE team (data capture via Apple iTunes Search API)
key_findings: 54 queries (9 terms x 6 storefronts, limit 50) returned 2,627 rows / 623 unique apps; stored as 08_ARAB_AUDIENCE_AND_CULTURE/_data/app_store_snapshot_2026-10-27.csv.

Ratings volume is dominated by Arabic word/trivia puzzle apps, not narrative mystery: e.g., كلمات كراش 373,462 ratings and ضربة معلم 286,459 in SA, versus the largest detective-titled game Harry Potter: Hogwarts Mystery 7,152 and Murder in Alps 4,179 in SA.

Across all 6 storefronts, titles in Arabic script that are mystery/detective games have tiny rating counts: لغز الجريمة 676 (SA) is the largest; the 2025-2026 Arabic investigation wave (القضية ٠٠١, تهمة, المفتش فهلوي, ورطة, فاكس) has 0-30 ratings each.

Total ratings on detective/mystery-titled apps per storefront: SA 39,118; AE 23,329; EG 12,893; KW 7,615; JO 3,755; MA 1,856 — i.e., Saudi Arabia shows the largest observable iOS audience for the genre.

Of ~150 detective/mystery-titled apps per storefront, only 25-32 declare Arabic support in their metadata, and the most-rated global mystery titles (Murder in Alps, Unsolved, Criminal Case on iOS, Murder Hornet) do not.
athar_applications: Primary quantitative demand proxy for G08: shows proven appetite for Arabic word/logic puzzles and for (non-Arabic) hidden-object mystery, but no proven Arabic narrative-mystery hit.
Baseline for monthly monitoring (re-run the same script on the same terms) to track the 2026 Arabic investigation-app wave.
limitations: Rating counts are a weak proxy for downloads (rating propensity differs by app and country) and are lifetime, not current.
iTunes Search results are relevance-ranked and capped at 50 per query; not a census; the heuristic category column is keyword-based and imperfect.
iOS skews to higher-income users (Gulf); Android dominates Egypt/Morocco, so EG/MA iOS counts understate those markets.
No age data: ratings cannot be attributed to 13-17s.

title: Google Play listing snapshot (gl=SA): install bands of 20 mystery/detective titles incl. Arabic ones, 2026-10-27
authors: ATHAR W2-AUDIENCE team (data capture from public Google Play listing pages)
publisher: Google LLC (Google Play public listing data)
key_findings: Global lifetime install bands: Criminal Case 100M+ (4.4, 4.26M reviews); Duskwood 10M+ (rated 16+); Murder in Alps 10M+; Unsolved 10M+; Homicide Squad 10M+; An Elmwood Trail 5M+ (4.8, 712K reviews); Who Is The Killer 5M+; Murder by Choice 5M+; Detective CrimeBot 1M+.
Arabic-original detective apps on Play: دائرة الشك 1K+ installs and ملف القضية: حقق في 1000 جريمة 500+ installs, both with no visible star rating (2026-10-27).
Text/chat-based narrative detective formats (Duskwood, An Elmwood Trail) reach 5-10M+ installs globally, showing the format scales on mobile.
athar_applications: Shows global ceiling for mobile narrative detective games and the near-zero traction of current Arabic-original attempts; positions ATHAR's challenge as quality/distribution rather than format viability.
limitations: Install bands are global, not per country, and are coarse (e.g., 10M+).
Selection of 20 titles is purposive (top results for Arabic queries on Play SA plus known Arabic titles), not a census.
Page scraping of public HTML; Google may vary markup.

title: Steam store tag counts (11 tags + all-games baseline) with vs without Arabic support, 2026-10-27 — extends ATH-SRC-0893
authors: ATHAR W2-AUDIENCE team (data capture from Steam store search)
key_findings: Of 186,322 games on Steam, 9,074 (4.9%) list Arabic support.

Detective tag: 5,312 games, 225 with Arabic (4.2%); Mystery 17,421 / 805 (4.6%); Investigation 6,443 / 217 (3.4%); Crime 3,125 / 136; Noir 2,310 / 105; Visual Novel 12,748 / 249 (2.0%); Interactive Fiction 9,331 / 230 (2.5%); Escape Room 983 / 66.
The most-reviewed Arabic-supporting Detective-tagged games include Return of the Obra Dinn, Phasmophobia, Tangle Tower and Disco Elysium – The Final Cut.
athar_applications: Quantifies the supply gap: narrative-heavy formats (Visual Novel, Interactive Fiction) are the least Arabic-localized, which is where ATHAR's text-heavy cases sit.
Supports positioning: Arabic narrative deduction is under-supplied on PC, but supply gap is not demand proof.
limitations: Supply-side data only; says nothing about Arab players' demand or purchases.
Steam 'supported language' is developer-declared and may mean interface-only.
Steam is PC-centric; teen MENA play is phone/console-first.
Detective-tag total (5,312) differs from ATH-SRC-0893 (4,858 with English filter) because of query parameters; Arabic count (225) matches.

title: إنترنت السعودية 2024 (Saudi Internet Report 2024)
publisher: Communications, Space and Technology Commission (CST), Saudi Arabia
key_findings: Official regulator data with a 10-19 age band: internet use 99.3% among 10-19-year-olds (national 99%).

Gaming platform use by age: among 10-19s, PlayStation 54.8% and smart devices (phones/tablets) 37.6%, Xbox 6.9%, Switch ~1.5%, Steam ~1.6%; nationally smart devices 24.2% and PlayStation 23.8% (females 28.5% smart devices vs males 21%; PlayStation males 30.2% vs females 15.1%).
Social apps among 10-19s: YouTube 84.5%, Snapchat 85.9%, TikTok 79.9%, WhatsApp 79%, Instagram 42.2%.
AI-tool use: 21.5% overall; 26.4% among 10-19s (27.3% among 20-29).

48.6% of internet users spend 7+ hours a day online; Madrasati (madrasati.sa) is among the 10 most-visited sites; most-downloaded phone games in 2024 were Whiteout Survival, Roblox, Subway Surfers, PUBG Mobile, Free Fire; Arabic trivia game جوابك جوابهم ranked 6th.
athar_applications: First official age-banded (10-19) Saudi data on platforms: consoles (PlayStation) lead teen gaming, phones second, so a phone-only ATHAR competes for 'secondary screen' time; consider tablet/web and console-adjacent session design.
Snapchat/YouTube/TikTok each reach ~80-86% of Saudi 10-19s: these are the acquisition channels; Instagram much weaker for teens.
Madrasati's top-10 traffic rank confirms the school platform as a mass-reach channel (relevant to G10).
limitations: Methodology (sample size, survey mode) not stated in the report; sources page lists 'CST studies', SensorTower and Ookla.
10-19 band mixes children and teens; no genre or time-on-games data; 'platform used' is not intensity.
Infographic report; some values read from bar charts.

title: Physical activity, screen time, dietary habits, and health outcomes among children and adolescents in the Middle East and North Africa region: a narrative review
key_findings: PRISMA-reported review of 18 studies (16 cross-sectional) from 7 countries (Saudi 7, Iran 3, Kuwait 3, Qatar 2, Oman, Morocco, Iraq), search 2012-2022.
Share of children/adolescents exceeding 2 h/day screen time ranges 21.9%-96.7%; e.g., Kuwait 14-19: ~96%; Saudi 14-19: 84% of males and 91.2% of females; Qatar 12-17: 43-62.5%; Morocco 13-18: ~40%.
No pooled estimate was possible because definitions, cut-offs and instruments differ; most data are self-reported.
athar_applications: Confirms that heavy screen exposure among Gulf teens is the norm, supporting bounded sessions and parent-facing 'healthy use' design; also shows ATHAR competes for already-saturated screen time.
limitations: Narrative review, not meta-analysis; no gaming/genre breakdown; data to 2022 only; Gulf-heavy; Iran is not Arab.

title: مسح استخدام وانتشار الاتصالات وتكنولوجيا المعلومات في المنازل 2024 — التقرير التحليلي (Household ICT Usage and Access Survey 2024, analytical report)
title_ar: مسح استخدام وانتشار الاتصالات وتكنولوجيا المعلومات في المنازل 2024
authors: Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship (Jordan)
publisher: Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship, Jordan
key_findings: Nationally representative household survey (8,270 households; annual since 2007; with confidence intervals and design effects): 95.6% of individuals aged 5+ used the internet in 2024; the highest use is in the 15-24 age group at 99.6%.
Smartphone ownership among 5-14-year-olds is ~50% (52% urban), versus ~96% among 15-19s (Table 1.1.14).
92.1% of individuals (95% CI 91.1-93.1) used the internet for entertainment/digital content including watching videos, music and playing or downloading electronic games (Table 9.30).
Households spend on average ~1.1% of monthly income on electronic games and hobbies (game software, video games, gaming apps/platforms, controllers), versus 6% on telecom services.
athar_applications: Official confirmation that 15-24 Jordanians are essentially universally online and that smartphone ownership jumps between the 10-14 and 15-19 bands: a 13-15 product must expect shared/parent devices for younger users.
Low household games spend share supports freemium/low-price tiers for the Levant.
limitations: Activities are not reported by age; gaming is bundled with other entertainment; no genre or time-use data.
Age bands do not isolate 13-17.

title: قائمة الأكثر مبيعًا في معرض القاهرة الدولي للكتاب 2026 (Cairo International Book Fair 2026 bestseller lists by publisher)
title_ar: قائمة الأكثر مبيعًا في معرض القاهرة الدولي للكتاب 2026
key_findings: Al-Dostour compiled top-5 sellers from 40+ public and private publishers at the 57th Cairo International Book Fair (published 6 Feb 2026).

At least 11 of the ~200 listed titles are explicitly crime/murder titles by Arab authors (e.g., جريمة في القصر الملكي، ثلاث غرف للقتل، جريمة على خشبة المسرح، قضية مخالب القط) and several more are horror/supernatural; Dar Dark's whole top-5 is horror/crime.
The Egyptian Pocket Novels publisher's top sellers still include Nabil Farouk's رجل المستحيل / ملف المستقبل and Ahmed Khaled Tawfik's ما وراء الطبيعة, decades after first publication.
athar_applications: Market signal that Arabic-original crime and horror fiction sells across many Egyptian publishers to a young-adult-leaning fair audience; supports Arabic narrative mystery as a culturally familiar genre (not a translated import).
Candidate partner/author pool for case writing (crime-novel publishers such as Dar Dark, Kayan, Rasm Bel Kalimat).
limitations: Self-reported by publishers to a newspaper; no unit sales, no audited data; genre classification is ours from titles only.
Fair visitors are not a representative reader sample; no age data.

title: لهذه الأسباب.. انتعاش سوق «أدب الرعب» في مصر (خاص)
title_ar: لهذه الأسباب.. انتعاش سوق «أدب الرعب» في مصر
key_findings: Publishers interviewed say horror was the best-selling category for them at the 2022 Cairo Book Fair and that young readers drive demand; one writer places detective/crime fiction next in popularity.
Interviewees credit Ahmed Khaled Tawfik (ما وراء الطبيعة, 1993) with building the young readership; others warn of oversupply and weak plotting.
athar_applications: Qualitative support that Egyptian youth reading culture favours suspense genres; ATHAR's differentiation should be fair-play deduction quality, not just 'dark' themes.
limitations: Interview-based journalism; no sales data or surveys.

title: Ministry of Culture unveils key findings of the 2023 UAE National Reading Index
publisher: Zawya (press release distribution of UAE Ministry of Culture)
key_findings: Sample: 3,800+ citizens and residents, 1,700+ students, 3,900+ teachers and parents, 150 writers.
Average books read per year rose to 7 (from 6 in 2021); online purchase is the main channel (53.4%).
Reading language: English 51% (up from 47.7%), Arabic only 24.6% (down from 26.6%), Arabic plus other languages 12.4%.
athar_applications: In the UAE, English reading dominates; an Arabic-first product there needs a bilingual (AR/EN) mode and cannot assume Arabic-reading preference, consistent with ATH-SRC-0707.
limitations: Press-release summary; no student-specific breakdown, no genre data; population includes large expatriate share.

title: «الإحصاء»: 81.6 % من السكان شاركوا ثقافياً.. والحدائق تتصدر (GASTAT Family Culture and Entertainment Survey: reading indicators 2024-2025)
title_ar: «الإحصاء»: 81.6 % من السكان شاركوا ثقافياً.. والحدائق تتصدر
authors: General Authority for Statistics (GASTAT), via Okaz
key_findings: GASTAT: 48.5% of the population read at least one book in 2024, falling to 33.7% in 2025; newspaper readers 38.2% (2024) and 26.8% (2025).
Non-Saudis read books and newspapers at higher rates than Saudis (no figures given in the article).
athar_applications: Book reading is a minority and declining activity in Saudi Arabia (population 15+), so ATHAR should not depend on a 'reader' identity; text load per screen must stay light and audio narration optional.
limitations: Newspaper report of GASTAT release; survey population 15+ (no teen breakdown); no genre data; definitions may differ between years.

title: Arabs in the region spend an average 35 hours on reading (Arab Reading Index findings)
key_findings: Arab Reading Index (presented at the MBRF Knowledge Summit): 148,000 respondents; average 35 hours of reading per year (15 work-related, 20 general) and ~16 books a year, of which ~7 school-related; digital reading exceeded print.
athar_applications: Useful only as a contested, self-selected benchmark; do not use in investor material without caveat.
limitations: Page dated 2018 in metadata though the index was released in 2016 (photo caption says Knowledge Summit 2016) — date ambiguity; self-selected sample; no methodology published in the article; no age or genre breakdown.

title: UNESCO Institute for Statistics (UIS) data API: enrolment in lower and upper secondary education, Arab states (indicators 20064, 20070), February 2026 data release
key_findings: Latest values (mostly 2024): lower+upper secondary enrolment — Egypt 11.56M (6.72M lower, 4.84M upper); Algeria 6.07M; Morocco 3.57M; Saudi Arabia 3.36M (1.66M lower, 1.70M upper); Syria 1.36M; Tunisia ~1.1M (mixed years); Jordan 1.03M; UAE 0.89M; Palestine 0.87M (2023); Oman 0.54M; Lebanon 0.42M; Qatar 0.15M; Bahrain 0.11M.
Kuwait's latest UIS value is 2012 (0.27M) and Yemen 2016, Sudan 2019 — gaps that must be filled from national sources.
Sum across the 16 queried Arab states ≈ 35.5M secondary students (mixed years), the base of a bottom-up sizing model.
athar_applications: Verified top-of-funnel input for the bottom-up 'Arab mystery-learning' sizing method in DEMAND_AND_MARKET_EVIDENCE.md (students x connectivity x willingness x price).
limitations: Secondary enrolment spans ~ages 12-18 (country-specific ISCED mapping), not exactly 13-17.
Different reference years across countries; API data version 20260507.
Reuse licence of UIS API data not verified in this session; check UIS terms of use before republishing numbers.

title: Ministry of Education (Saudi Arabia) — E-learning Service: Madrasati platform
authors: Ministry of Education, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
key_findings: Official service page: Madrasati launched 2020, free, Arabic, portal and mobile app; more than 6 million student beneficiaries.
Features include a Learning Resources Room (My Courses, Reading Club, Games Room), an enrichment bank, virtual labs, central tests and teacher-student messaging.
athar_applications: The existence of an official 'Games Room' and 'enrichment bank' inside Madrasati defines the concrete B2G slot ATHAR would target in Saudi Arabia (enrichment content for the Critical Thinking subject), subject to MoE approval.
Madrasati is also a top-10 visited site in Saudi Arabia (ATH-SRC-1503), confirming reach.
limitations: Page does not describe how third-party content enters the enrichment bank or Games Room, or any vendor approval route; no update date.

title: Ministry of Education (Saudi Arabia) — Tenders and Procurements (Etimad)
authors: Ministry of Education, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
key_findings: The Saudi MoE publishes its competitions and purchases on Etimad, the Ministry of Finance's government e-procurement system; suppliers search by government entity to see open and closed tenders, documents and results.
athar_applications: Procurement path for Saudi public-school content is formal tendering via Etimad (or via MoE-affiliated companies); ATHAR should monitor closed MoE tenders for 'digital content'/'enrichment' to learn typical scope and price ranges.
limitations: No information on digital-content-specific procedures, eligibility, or the role of MoE-affiliated companies.

title: Saudi Arabia Country Commercial Guide — Selling to the Public Sector
authors: International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce
key_findings: Amended Government Tenders and Procurement Law (2019) governs public contracts; Etimad (launched 2018 by the Ministry of Finance) consolidates bidding and, as a general rule, all government procurements must be listed there.
Preference for Saudi and majority-Saudi-owned suppliers; GCC products up to 10% price preference; local-content quotas by sector.

Since 1 January 2024, companies bidding on Etimad tenders must hold a Saudi regional headquarters (RHQ) licence (15 FTE in year one, incl. 3 C-suite) per a December 2023 Council of Ministers resolution.
athar_applications: A non-Saudi ATHAR entity cannot bid directly on most MoE tenders without a Saudi RHQ or a local partner; B2G entry in Saudi Arabia should go through a Saudi-registered partner or a pilot via MoE-affiliated channels.
limitations: Secondary summary by a foreign government (last published 2026-05-19); verify against Saudi primary texts (MoF GTPL) before contracting; RHQ rule has exemptions not covered here.

title: Alef Education Holding plc announces its intention to list on the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange
key_findings: Long-term contract with Abu Dhabi's Department of Education and Knowledge (ADEK): minimum 80,000 students at a fixed fee per student, seven years remaining at IPO (May 2024).
Platform reaches all UAE public schools with 100% penetration in Cycle 2 (grades 5-8) and Cycle 3 (grades 9-12); 40-50% of the private-school market.
2023 revenue AED 750M (from AED 667M in 2021); adjusted EBITDA margin 65%; ~1.1M registered students, 50,000 teachers, 7,000 schools including Indonesia (~650,000 students) and a Morocco pilot.
athar_applications: Shows the dominant UAE public-school EdTech model is a per-student government contract held by an incumbent with 100% secondary penetration: ATHAR's UAE school route is more realistic as content partner/module on such a platform than as a stand-alone vendor.
Benchmark for B2G per-student pricing logic (fee per student, minimum volumes).
limitations: Issuer marketing at IPO; per-student fee not disclosed; date of page inferred from IPO timeline.

title: Alef Education lifts profit and maintains 73% margin on global momentum
key_findings: 9M-2025: revenue AED 572.8M (+4%), EBITDA AED 418M (73% margin), net profit AED 364.7M.
More than 73,000 public-school learners on the platform (ADEK) and 180 private schools with 122,000 paying students (~35% of UAE private market); six new B2B/government contracts worth AED 57M.
athar_applications: Indicates slow growth (3-4% revenue guidance) of a mature incumbent — the UAE school EdTech market is consolidated; ATHAR should treat UAE schools as partnership, not greenfield.
limitations: Journalism summarising company results; public-learner figure (73,000) differs in scope from the IPO 'minimum 80,000' contract — definitions unclear.

title: Alef Education and the Ministry of Education in UAE inaugurate implementation of Alef Education System in 10 Abu Dhabi public schools
key_findings: June 2018 MoE-Alef agreement extended a 2017 single-school pilot to 10 Abu Dhabi public schools (6,000+ students, grades 6-8) from September 2018, with an onsite implementation team.
Path: one-school pilot -> 10-school agreement -> later national scale (see ATH-SRC-1515).
athar_applications: Documented B2G adoption path in the UAE: pilot in one public school with outcome data, then ministry agreement. ATHAR's school route should plan a measured pilot first.
limitations: No financial terms; 2018 context; MoE/ADEK roles changed since.

title: Introduction of critical thinking course in Saudi curriculum hailed as 'ground-breaking'
key_findings: Describes the critical thinking and philosophy course that launched in 2021 (announced 2018): lessons pose hard social questions for students to answer in their own words; the introduction uses the story of Galileo; examples include a case study on the Charlie Hebdo cartoons.
An IMPACT-se review (Marcus Sheff) called the course a major step; stated government goal was tolerance and reducing intellectual extremism.
athar_applications: Indicates the Saudi course is philosophy- and discussion-oriented (open questions, case studies) rather than formal logic drills — ATHAR's evidence-reasoning cases would complement it with structured inference practice; alignment must still be checked against official outcomes.
limitations: Journalism based on an advocacy NGO's textbook review (IMPACT-se); not the official outcomes document; grades and hours not stated.

title: Call for Media Literacy in Egyptian School Curricula Gets Positive Response
key_findings: August 2026: MP Dr. Thuraya El-Badawy asked Egypt's Ministry of Education and Technical Education to add media literacy and critical thinking to basic education; a Ministry report reportedly called the recommendations very important and urgent.

The Ministry says media-literacy topics are already in curricula and printed textbooks; a committee of curriculum and educational-media experts was formed; integration across Arabic, ICT, science, maths, art and social studies is described as the most feasible immediate option; no decision or timeline yet.
athar_applications: Egypt has no stand-alone critical-thinking subject yet; the near-term opening is cross-curricular 'misinformation/media literacy' activities — ATHAR's verification-case line fits this framing better than 'critical thinking course alignment'.
limitations: Based largely on the MP's account of a ministry report, not a published ministry document; no grades or dates.

title: 'We are in a phase as big as the printing press': How Jordan became Arab world's blueprint for media literacy
key_findings: Jordan formally adopted media and information literacy (MIL) as a government priority in 2019; first National MIL Strategy 2020-2023 (described as the first comprehensive formal MIL plan in an Arab country); second strategy 2026-2029 launched late 2025.

MIL concepts are integrated into school curricula across religion, social sciences and Arabic, with a gap between integration and classroom practice; Jordan Media Institute and UNESCO are key partners.
athar_applications: Jordan is the clearest Arab policy home for 'verification/fact-checking' cases; the Jordan Media Institute is a credible pilot partner (see also ATH-SRC-1135).
limitations: Journalism; no school/student counts.

title: Jordan Is a Leader in Media Literacy but Experts Say There Is More to Do
key_findings: Opinion piece: media literacy taught in some Jordanian schools since 2016, introduced in roughly 100 schools as an additional subject or extracurricular activity; not mandatory; only a small share of teachers receive specialised training; remote areas lag.
athar_applications: Teacher-capacity gap means ATHAR's school offer must include a ready-to-run teacher guide; 'extracurricular club' is the realistic Jordanian entry format.
limitations: Opinion article; figures not sourced to the ministry.

title: Discovery Education and Private Sector Partnerships: Interview with Emily Waters (chapter 14 in Education 2.0: Chronicles of Technological and Cultural Change in Egypt)
key_findings: Egypt's Education 2.0 reform (from 2017) used an international private partner (Discovery Education) to co-produce textbooks, teacher guides, digital content and teacher PD with the Ministry, delivered at speed with Egyptian counterpart teams.
athar_applications: Egyptian public-school content has been sourced through large strategic partnerships rather than open marketplaces; a small vendor would need to enter via such partners or via the Egyptian Knowledge Bank.
limitations: Interview chapter (practitioner perspective); no contract terms or evaluation data on this page.

title: Qatar — TIMSS 2019 Encyclopedia chapter (Education Policy and Curriculum in Mathematics and Science)
publisher: TIMSS & PIRLS International Study Center, Boston College (IEA)
key_findings: The Qatar National Curriculum Framework uses a competency-based approach; key competencies listed for mathematics include Creative and Critical Thinking, Inquiry and Research and Problem Solving; science lists Inquiry and Research and Critical and Creative Thinking.
athar_applications: Qatar frames critical thinking as a cross-curricular competency (not a separate subject): ATHAR alignment claims there should map to QNCF competencies within science/maths.
limitations: Describes 2018-era curriculum documents; does not cover digital-content procurement; edu.gov.qa still unverified (robots-blocked).

title: A Large and Balanced Corpus for Fine-grained Arabic Readability Assessment (BAREC)
publisher: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2025
key_findings: BAREC: 69,441 sentences (>1M words) manually annotated on a 19-level readability scale from kindergarten to postgraduate comprehension, balanced across genres, topics and audiences.
Average pairwise inter-annotator agreement (quadratic weighted kappa) reported as 81.8%; corpus, annotation guidelines and benchmark models released openly.
athar_applications: The most credible current tool to calibrate ATHAR case text by level: run each case's narration through a BAREC-trained model and set targets per age band (13-15 vs 16-18) instead of the ad-hoc '20-word sentence' rule.
Answers G09 sub-question 'which Arabic readability instrument?' provisionally; a linguist should validate level targets.
limitations: Levels are sentence-level and MSA-focused; mapping to school grades/ages not given on the abstract page; dialect dialogue not covered.
Corpus licence not confirmed on the fetched page.

title: DARES: Dataset for Arabic Readability Estimation of School Materials
publisher: Proceedings of the Workshop on DeTermIt! Evaluating Text Difficulty in a Multilingual Context @ LREC-COLING 2024 (ELRA and ICCL)
key_findings: 13,335 text instances from Saudi school textbooks (2021) labelled by educational level and by grade.
Best model (CAMeLBERTmix) reached weighted F1 0.91 for coarse level (primary/secondary) but only 0.68 (macro 0.55) for exact grade.
athar_applications: Grade-anchored to the Saudi curriculum — useful to check that ATHAR text for 13-15 sits at or below Saudi intermediate-grade textbook difficulty.
Shows automatic grade prediction is unreliable at single-grade precision; use bands, not exact grades.
limitations: Saudi textbooks only; textbook language differs from narrative fiction; DOI not shown on page.

title: Arabic diglossia: advocating for a non-deficit model in comparative analysis of reading and language acquisition
key_findings: Narrative mini-review of 12 studies (K-12, mainly Northern Palestinian dialect speakers): children perform better on spoken-Arabic-shared elements than MSA-only elements in early grades, but phonological/lexical distance effects shrink and sometimes disappear by late elementary school.

Abu-Liel, Ibrahim & Eviatar (2021), with 77 eighth graders aged 13-15 (North Palestinian dialects), found unvowelled MSA read fastest/most accurately, vowelled MSA slowest, Arabizi in between, while vowelled MSA gave the best comprehension. [Clarified 2026-10-27 by deep-card review: the study is an adolescent sample.]
Argues against a 'deficit' framing: diglossia alone does not explain weak reading outcomes.
athar_applications: Supports the assumption that by 13+ the MSA decoding penalty is small; the remaining risk for teens is vocabulary/register (engagement), not decoding — so ATHAR's G09 test should measure enjoyment and completion more than raw comprehension.
Supports selective (not full) vowelling for clue-critical words.
limitations: Few eligible studies, one regional dialect group; only one adolescent reading study (Abu-Liel et al. 2021, grade 8) and no adolescent preference/enjoyment data. [Corrected 2026-10-27 by deep-card review.]

title: Arabic Language Diglossia — A Systematic Review (Final Findings & Recommendations)
authors: Queen Rania Foundation (commissioned; research team at Zayed University)
key_findings: QRF-commissioned (2020) mixed-method review of 156 studies and conceptual papers: MSA difficulty decreases with exposure, proficiency and grade (notably around Grade 4); socio-economic factors can delay MSA learning; some studies find no effect of diglossia on school performance — overall evidence inconclusive.
Recommends more MSA exposure through quality media and reading, and more intervention research.
athar_applications: Positions ATHAR's MSA narration as 'quality MSA exposure' (a parent/school-friendly benefit) while acknowledging no direct teen evidence.
limitations: Blog summary of the final findings; full report not located; publication date not stated; individual authors not named.

title: Disney Translates 'Frozen' Into A More Formal Arabic
key_findings: Frozen (2014 release) was Disney's first animated feature dubbed into Modern Standard Arabic after decades of Egyptian-dialect dubs (e.g., The Lion King, Snow White).
Commentator Elias Muhanna linked the change to a 2013 Al Jazeera-Disney children's programming deal requiring classical Arabic; audience reaction was mixed.
athar_applications: Historical evidence that register choice in Arab children's media is driven by distributor/broadcaster policy as much as by audience preference — relevant to ATHAR's school/broadcast partners demanding MSA.
limitations: Journalism/interview; reasons are commentator interpretation, not Disney statement.

title: Egyptian Disney fans ask for return to dubbing in Egyptian Arabic dialect
key_findings: April 2016: hashtag campaigns and an online petition asked Disney to return to Egyptian-dialect dubbing ahead of Finding Dory; trended in Egypt and the wider Arab world; Disney had earlier said MSA targets the whole Arab world.
athar_applications: Evidence of strong audience attachment to Egyptian-dialect voices in entertainment — supports a later Egyptian-dialect voice pack as an engagement lever.
limitations: No numbers on petition size; Egypt-centric; adult fans, not teen-specific.

title: Disney to dub new film Encanto in Egyptian Arabic after 10-year hiatus
key_findings: March 2022: Disney released an Egyptian-Arabic dub of Encanto in addition to the standard-Arabic version, ending a ~10-year MSA-only period that began around 2012.
A fan-page administrator attributed the change to persistent audience demand and the imminent Disney+ MENA launch.
athar_applications: The market converged on a dual-track model (MSA + Egyptian dialect versions) — mirrors ATHAR's 'two layers and a half' plan: MSA base plus optional dialect voice packs, with Egyptian as the first candidate.
limitations: Journalism quoting a fan-page admin, not Disney; Moana Egyptian edition (2017) shows earlier exceptions (see ATH-SRC-1531).

title: Disney Is Releasing an Egyptian Dialect Edition of Moana featuring Carmen Soliman
key_findings: March 2017: Disney announced a full Egyptian-dialect edition of Moana (songs by Carmen Soliman), reported as a first response to the 'Disney in Egyptian' campaign.
athar_applications: Corrects the '10-year hiatus' framing in ATH-SRC-1530: dialect editions re-appeared selectively from 2017.
limitations: Lifestyle-media report; does not state whether an MSA version co-existed.

title: From Roots to Relevance: Making Arabic the language of opportunity for MENA's young people
authors: Congress of Arabic & Creative Industries / Abu Dhabi Arabic Language Centre
publisher: Abu Dhabi Arabic Language Centre (Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi), with Strategy&
key_findings: Ipsos/ALC Arab Youth Pulse Survey 2025: 4,092 respondents aged 18-25 in 10 countries (Bahrain, Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Syria, UAE).
71% prefer media in Arabic; 67% say Arabic content feels dated compared with English content; 77% say English is essential for their goals; 70% switch languages by context.
Factors that would increase Arabic use: better Arabic education 38%, more Arabic online content 34%, better Arabic app interfaces 32%, more creative Arabic content 30%.
athar_applications: Directly reframes the 2023 '54% say Arabic matters less' signal: young Arabs prefer Arabic media but judge it dated — the opportunity is modern, high-quality Arabic content, which is ATHAR's positioning.
Supports a polished Arabic UI and bilingual switch (code-switching is normal).
limitations: 18-25 only (no 13-17); online method not detailed in fetched text; MSA vs dialect not separated; commissioned by a language-promotion body (possible framing bias); publication date inferred (2026).

title: Young Arabs want more Arabic content – but say much of it feels outdated
key_findings: Reports the Congress ACI Arab Youth Pulse Survey 2025 (Ipsos with Abu Dhabi Arabic Language Centre; 4,092 aged 18-25; 10 countries) at the 5th Congress of Arabic and Creative Industries (Sept 2026): 71% prefer Arabic media; 67% find Arabic content outdated vs English; Arabic used by 91% at home, 64% at school/work.
athar_applications: Independent press confirmation of ATH-SRC-1532 findings and their release date.
limitations: Journalism; same survey as 1532.

title: A descriptive analysis of the choice between modern standard Arabic and Egyptian dialect in the dubbed versions of Disney animated films
publisher: University of Geneva (Archive ouverte UNIGE), Faculty of Translation and Interpreting
key_findings: Master's thesis describing Disney's shift from Egyptian dialect to MSA and the later return to dual releases (MSA and Egyptian), based on Disney films and interviews with two dubbing-industry figures; concludes choices track linguistic change and market forces.
athar_applications: Academic confirmation of the dual-register trajectory in Arabic children's dubbing.
limitations: Master's thesis; full text restricted; two interviews only.

title: Parental mediation of adolescents' Internet use in Jordan
publisher: Journal of Arab & Muslim Media Research (Intellect)
key_findings: Survey of 400 Jordanian preparatory and secondary students (grades 7-12) on parental mediation strategies (restrictive, instructive, co-use) and exposure to online risks.

Boys were more exposed to online risks; mother's education level significantly affected instructive mediation and risk exposure, father's education affected co-use; no gender effect on restrictive or instructive mediation.
athar_applications: First verified Levant parental-mediation study for 13-17: instructive (explaining) mediation is the lever tied to parental education — ATHAR's parent tools should give low-literacy-friendly conversation prompts, not just controls.
limitations: 2014 data (pre-TikTok era); single country; abstract-level reading only; sampling details not read.

title: استراتيجيات الوساطة الأبوية في استخدام المراهقين للأنترنت في الجزائر (Parental Mediation strategies in adolescent Internet use in Algeria)
title_ar: استراتيجيات الوساطة الأبوية في استخدام المراهقين للأنترنت في الجزائر
publisher: International Journal of Social Communication (Abdelhamid Ibn Badis University of Mostaganem)
key_findings: Likert questionnaire, convenience sample of 72, focused on adolescents aged 12-15 (vol. 10 no. 4, pp. 443-459).
Algerian parents reportedly use active mediation to a very high degree and restrictive mediation to a high degree (four strategies examined: active, participation, restrictive, technical).
athar_applications: Weak but only verified Maghreb signal: active (dialogue) mediation is the parents' self-reported default — consistent with ATHAR's 'conversation not surveillance' parent design.
limitations: Very small convenience sample; unclear whether respondents were parents or adolescents; local journal without DOI; self-report.

title: The Impact of Screen Exposure on Children in Morocco
publisher: International Journal of Health Sciences (CARI Journals)
key_findings: Cross-sectional parent questionnaire (333 parents; 590 children aged 3 months-12 years): 93% of parents use screens in front of their child; 56% of children have 2-4 h daily exposure; in 60% of cases an adult must intervene to stop screen time.
athar_applications: Indicates Moroccan parents' main concern is screen time and self-regulation, not content genre — ATHAR's bounded-session design addresses the primary parental worry there.
limitations: Under-12s only; small regional sample; low-visibility journal; no teen or content-attitude data.

title: Online Protection, Agency, and Wellbeing for Adolescent Girls and Boys in the MENA Region
authors: Save the Children Middle East, North Africa and Eastern Europe Regional Office
key_findings: Qualitative study with adolescents aged 10-17 and caregivers in four provinces of Lebanon and Türkiye (Nov 2023).

Children start using the internet around age five; smartphones are the main device, making supervision harder; risks include inappropriate/imitation-prone content, economic abuse, fraud, cyberbullying and abuse on social, gaming and networking platforms.
athar_applications: Caregiver concern centres on contact risks and inappropriate content on open platforms — ATHAR's closed, chat-free (or moderated) design and no stranger contact is a parent-facing selling point in the Levant.
limitations: Qualitative; abstract-level reading; Lebanon mixed with Türkiye; no N reported on landing page.

title: Jordan bans online game PUBG over 'negative effects'
key_findings: July 2019: Jordan's Telecommunications Regulatory Authority blocked PUBG citing negative effects on users; local psychologists had warned it encourages violence and bullying among youth.
athar_applications: Levant regulators act on perceived youth-harm from violent games; ATHAR must keep violence off-screen and frame cases as reasoning, not combat, to avoid being lumped with 'violent games'.
limitations: Based on an unnamed TRA source; ban status later not verified here.

title: Iraq parliament unanimously bans PUBG, Fortnite for 'inciting violence'
key_findings: April 2019: Iraq's parliament unanimously voted to block games that 'incite violence' (named PUBG and Fortnite), saying they threaten social security, morals, civics and education; a full ban required cabinet approval.
athar_applications: Public-moral framing of games as a threat to youth is strong in parts of the region; ATHAR's marketing must lead with education and family values, and avoid 'crime game' wording.
limitations: Journalism; implementation and later status not verified.

title: Saudi Arabia captures 20% of MENA gaming revenues: Savvy report
key_findings: Reporting Savvy Games' 2024 report: MENA video-games revenue US$5.62B in 2024, forecast US$6.94B by 2027 (7.3% CAGR 2024-2027); Saudi Arabia ~20% (~US$1.19B), forecast US$1.64B by 2028 (8.2% CAGR); 25.81M+ Saudi gamers.
Methodology not stated in the article; global forecast lines in the same piece come from Mordor Intelligence, not Savvy.
athar_applications: Top-down ceiling for G26: total MENA games spend ~US$5.6B (2024). Any 'mystery-learning' revenue is a tiny slice; use only as context, never as ATHAR's addressable market.
limitations: Secondary press report of an issuer-adjacent (PIF-owned Savvy) report; definitions (MENA scope, includes hardware?) unknown; contrasts with Niko's MENA-3 US$2.0B (2024, 3 countries only) [ATH-SRC-0719].

title: Saudi Arabia's esports sector poised for $13.3bn boost by 2030 (PwC Middle East with Saudi Esports Federation)
key_findings: PwC Middle East analysis with the Saudi Esports Federation: esports could add US$13.3B to Saudi GDP and ~39,000 jobs by 2030; Middle East & Africa gaming revenues ~US$7.2B in 2023; 23.5M Saudi 'gaming enthusiasts' (67% of population).
athar_applications: Context only: shows the policy weight behind gaming in Saudi Arabia; not an EdTech or mystery-genre number.
limitations: Report title not given; MEA (incl. Africa/Türkiye?) scope differs from MENA; GDP-contribution figures are policy projections.

title: UAE gaming market sees rapid growth as video games dominate digital spending
key_findings: An unnamed 'industry study' (data from Statista, DataReportal, GSMA Intelligence, SimilarWeb) puts 2024 video-game consumer spend in KSA+UAE+Egypt at ~US$2.52B; UAE US$421M; Egypt ~US$1.10B; games = 63.2% of digital media spend in the three markets.
athar_applications: Do NOT use for sizing: listed only to document conflicting numbers (Egypt US$1.10B here vs Egypt ARPU US$3.39 in Niko [ATH-SRC-0719]).
limitations: Publisher of the study not named; derived from aggregator estimates; internally inconsistent with Niko Partners; grade E (review list only).

title: 2025 Middle East & North Africa EdTech 50
key_findings: 11 Nov 2025 list of 50 young MENA EdTechs scored by HolonIQ: Saudi Arabia ~one-third of the cohort (now largest, overtaking Egypt), Egypt ~one-quarter, UAE 18%.
K-12 is 44% of the cohort; more than half are direct-to-consumer, ~one-third B2B.
No MENA EdTech market-size figure is published on the page.
athar_applications: Shows where EdTech company formation is concentrated (KSA > Egypt > UAE) and that K-12 D2C is the dominant model; no regional 'game-based reasoning' category exists — confirms white space but also the lack of a sized market.
limitations: Ranking/landscape, not market sizing; selection criteria partly qualitative.

title: EdTech in MENA: The Community and the Cloud
key_findings: MAGNiTT verified-deal data to Nov 2021: MENA EdTech funding grew four consecutive years from 2018; 2021 a record year; ~75% of EdTech deals early-stage; Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Jordan led deal counts (Jordan 14 EdTech deals 2020-21).
Arabic-content startups with investor traction named: Abjjad and Wajeez (Jordan), Zedny (Egypt), Aanab (Saudi Arabia).
athar_applications: Investor context: Arabic-content and K-12 EdTech is fundable mainly at early stage; ATHAR's raise should be sized accordingly.
limitations: 2021 snapshot; growth given as percentages without absolute baseline; pre-2022 funding downturn.

title: Abjjad raises $1 million in Series A
key_findings: Dec 2020: Jordan-based Abjjad (founded 2012) raised US$1M Series A; 6,000+ Arabic e-books; subscription US$5.99/month; 1.5M registered readers and writers (company claim).
athar_applications: Benchmark for Arabic digital-reading subscription pricing (~US$6/month) and scale (1.5M registered, paying share unknown); a mystery-case subscription in the same price band is plausible for Gulf/Levant.
limitations: Company claims via startup press; registered ≠ paying; 2020 data.

title: Abjjad — 'روايات بوليسية' (detective novels) category listing
key_findings: On 2026-10-27 the detective-novel category listed 1,483 books; the first page mixes Arab authors (Shahd Qurban's 005 series, Yahya Azzam, Nuha Dawoud x3, Ahmed Mourad) with translated Christie, Conan Doyle, Hawkins, Turton.
Abjjad's iOS app: 6,741 ratings (SA), 3,025 (EG), 443 (JO), avg ~4.6-4.7 (iTunes lookup, 2026-10-27).
athar_applications: Evidence of an active contemporary Arabic-original detective-fiction supply (e.g., Nuha Dawoud's crime series) — potential writers and cross-promotion partners.
limitations: Listing order criterion unknown (popularity vs recency); no reader counts; platform audience skews adult.

title: Le CESE alerte sur l'absence d'un cadre réglementaire 'efficace' pour protéger les enfants sur les plateformes numériques
key_findings: Morocco's Economic, Social and Environmental Council (CESE) opinion 'Pour un environnement numérique inclusif et protecteur des enfants' (adopted unanimously March 2024; presented 30 Jan 2025): 97% of under-18s used social platforms in 2024; two in three children have access to social networks.

Ouchariko citizen consultation: 69% worried about children's social-media use; 58% think platforms are not beneficial for young people; 42% think they could be positive from age 15; 88% want digital education integrated into school curricula.
Recommends a national child-online-protection observatory, awareness campaigns for parents and children, safety-by-design guidelines and tighter rules on children's data.
athar_applications: Maghreb parents' concern is high and they explicitly want digital/critical education in schools (88%) — supports positioning ATHAR as 'digital-literacy through cases' for Moroccan schools and parents.
Safety-by-design and data-minimisation are policy expectations in Morocco, aligning with library 11.
limitations: Consultation is self-selected online (Ouchariko), not representative; journalism summary of the opinion; no game-specific data.

title: Près de 70% des Marocains « inquiets » quant à l'utilisation des réseaux sociaux par les enfants
key_findings: CESE Ouchariko consultation (934 participants, mostly urban university graduates): 66.97% of parents worried about sexual/pornographic content, 55.51% about hate and violence messages, 46.07% about cyberbullying; 47.65% say their children have a personal smartphone, mostly obtained after age 12.
athar_applications: Parental worry ranking (sexual content > hate/violence > bullying) suggests mystery content is acceptable if it avoids sexual content and graphic violence and has no open chat — consistent with ATHAR's content policy.
limitations: Non-representative online sample; journalism; gender breakdown in article does not sum to 100%.

title: TIC : les marocains sont hyperconnectés (ANRT ICT indicators survey, first results)
key_findings: ANRT annual ICT survey (12,000 households/individuals; 2017 data): 98.4% of 15-24 internet users on social networks; 80% of 5-39-year-olds own a smartphone; over 7 in 10 parents say they lack tools to guide their children's internet use.
athar_applications: Older but official-survey signal that Moroccan parents feel unequipped — supports simple, guided parent tools in French/Arabic.
limitations: 2017 data reported in 2018 press; superseded by later ANRT waves not verified here.

title: Apple Podcasts top-100 charts snapshot in six Arab storefronts (SA, EG, AE, MA, JO, KW), chart dated 2026-10-26
authors: ATHAR W2-AUDIENCE team (data capture via Apple iTunes RSS toppodcasts feed)
key_findings: The Arabic True Crime show سوالف طريق (Abu Talal Al-Hamrani) is #1 overall on Apple Podcasts in Saudi Arabia, UAE and Kuwait, #2 in Jordan, #41 in Morocco and #61 in Egypt (chart of 2026-10-26).

Other Arabic crime/story shows in the overall top-100: قصص من المحاكم (#15 SA, #29 JO), قضية (#54 SA), صندوق الجرائم (#95 EG, #98 JO), ملفات بولـيسية (#42 MA); fiction-drama قصص رون is top-30 in five of six storefronts.
Arabic-script titles make up 78-82 of the top-100 in SA, EG and JO but 36 in the UAE; Morocco's chart includes many French true-crime shows.
athar_applications: Strongest direct demand signal found for Arabic crime/mystery *narrative*: story-led crime audio tops national charts across the Gulf and Levant — narrative crime appetite is proven in audio, though for adults and real cases.
Suggests an audio-first 'case narration' format and podcast partnerships (with strict fictional-case framing for minors).
limitations: Chart rank reflects recent velocity, not audience size; Apple Podcasts share is small vs YouTube/Spotify/Anghami; audience age unknown (likely adult); real-crime content is not suitable as-is for 13-17.

title: سوالف طريق - ابو طلال الحمراني (Apple Podcasts show page)
key_findings: Real-life stories 'for entertainment and lessons' with listener-submitted stories (voice notes/text); ~1.9k episodes since 2023; episodes ~22-40 min; 4.0 from ~1,255 ratings (SA); category True Crime.
athar_applications: Format lessons: high-frequency, short (20-35 min) episodes in Gulf dialect with a moral 'lesson' framing and audience participation — a culturally accepted crime-story framing (عبرة) that ATHAR can borrow for fictional cases.
limitations: Show page only; audience size/age unknown; dialect content; real cases.

title: «الإنجليزية» في أولى ابتدائي.. و«التفكير الناقد» في المتوسطة
title_ar: «الإنجليزية» في أولى ابتدائي.. و«التفكير الناقد» في المتوسطة
key_findings: 26 May 2021: Saudi MoE's developed study plans (three-semester system) allocate Critical Thinking 2 periods per week in grade 3 intermediate (grade 9) and 4 periods per week in the secondary stage.
Same plans added English from grade 1, digital skills in grades 4-6, life and family skills, and made the activity period a core subject.
athar_applications: Gives the classroom time budget for alignment design: a grade-9 class has ~2 x 45-min periods/week for Critical Thinking — an ATHAR classroom case should fit one period (≈35-40 min of play + debrief) or a two-period mini-unit.
Secondary allocation (4/week) allows a multi-period case project.
limitations: 2021 newspaper report; allocations may have changed in 1446-1448 plans (see ATH-SRC-0758, ATH-SRC-0760); does not state semester or track placement.

title: Egypt Pushes for Stricter Online Rules to Protect Children
key_findings: Jan 2026: Egypt's National Council for Childhood and Motherhood called regulating children's use of phones, social media and electronic games central to national child-protection policy; Parliament announced plans to draft a law on children's social-media use.
Cites a 2024 National Center for Social and Criminological Research report that about half of Egyptian under-18s use social media.
athar_applications: Egyptian regulation of children's games/social apps is being drafted in 2026 — ATHAR's Egypt launch should anticipate age-verification, parental-consent and contact-restriction rules (coordinate with library 11, G01).
Positions ATHAR as 'protective, educational' content in a tightening policy climate.
limitations: Journalism aggregating other outlets; no draft-law text; no gaming statistics.

title: 6.72M students, over 513,000 teachers in general education: Ministry
key_findings: Oct 2024 (MoE figures via its official X account): 6,718,530 general-education students, 513,120 teachers, 36,800 schools.
Intermediate stage 1,571,960 students (120,030 teachers); secondary stage 1,457,650 students (120,810 teachers).
athar_applications: National (MoE) count for the Saudi sizing node: ~1.57M intermediate students; grade 9 (the Critical Thinking grade) ≈ one-third of intermediate ≈ ~0.5M students (estimate by division, to be replaced by MoE grade-level data).
~120,000 intermediate teachers = teacher-facing B2B/B2G audience.
limitations: Secondary report of an MoE social-media post; public/private split not given; primary-stage boys/girls figures in the article look inconsistent (2.1M girls vs 1.16M boys) — treat stage totals as indicative; UIS gives 1.66M lower-secondary (ATH-SRC-1511).

title: Prevalence of video gaming disorder in Saudi Arabia: a school-based national study
publisher: Journal of the Egyptian Public Health Association (Springer Open)
key_findings: National school-based survey, all Saudi regions, 2021-2022, multistage stratified cluster sampling: 5,332 intermediate and secondary students (mean age 15.5); 82.2% (4,385) play video games, 17.8% do not.
Among gamers: 92.5% play online; devices — smartphone 66.2%, console 57.5%, multiple devices 37.9%, PC 15.8%, tablet 11.4%.
Game categories played (multiple answers): fighting 47.8%, adventure 42.0%, multiplayer 38.5%, sports 33.2%, car racing 26.9%, puzzle 26.7%, war 26.0%.
Gaming disorder (DSM-5-based 9-item scale ≥5) 20.45%; linked to multiple devices, online, fighting, racing, war, adventure and multiplayer games — not to puzzle or sports games or mobile-only play.
athar_applications: Best available representative-design data on Saudi 13-18 gaming: ~8 in 10 teens game; 'puzzle' is a minority category (~27%) while adventure (42%) — the closest umbrella for narrative mystery — is common: position ATHAR as story-adventure + deduction, not 'puzzle app'.
Puzzle and mobile-only play were not associated with disorder — supports a parent-facing 'healthy gaming' claim for a bounded, mobile, puzzle-reasoning product (as association only).
limitations: Genre list has no 'mystery/detective' or 'story' category; self-report; 2021-22 data; Saudi only; GD scale cut-offs debated.

title: What Drives Saudi Gamers? A Study of Gender, Genre, and Geography
key_findings: Online survey of 397 Saudi nationals (62.2% female; 42.8% aged 18-24) using an Arabic Gamer Motivation Profile: most-selected genres Action 52.5%, Adventure 51.7%, Multiplayer 46.4%, Puzzle 45.3%, Simulation 32.1%, Open World 31.7%; 58.9% play board/card games (e.g., Baloot, Jackaroo).
Women scored higher on Social and Immersion motivations, men on Action and Mastery; regional differences modest.
athar_applications: Immersion and social motivations (stronger among women, who are >60% of this sample) fit narrative co-op mystery; social table games (Baloot) suggest a 'majlis' group-play mode, echoing Saudi group-investigation apps (ATH-SRC-1158, ATH-SRC-1159).
limitations: Convenience online sample skewed female and young adult; no under-18 data stated; no mystery-genre category; reported df inconsistencies.

title: Mohammed bin Rashid to crown winners of Arab Reading Challenge 2025
key_findings: 9th edition (2025): over 32 million participating students from 50 countries, 132,112 schools and 161,004 supervisors; participants read and summarise 50 books a year.
athar_applications: The largest school-based Arabic reading-promotion network: a potential distribution/partnership channel (e.g., 'case files' as summarisable reading) and evidence that ministries and schools mobilise at scale for Arabic reading.
limitations: Official promotional figures (registrations, not completions); participation is often school-driven; age range not stated on page.

title: 21 titles from 8 countries shortlisted for Dh1.2 million award for Arabic Children's Literature (Etisalat Award, 15th edition)
key_findings: 15th Etisalat Award (UAEBBY, 2023): 323 submissions, of which only 49 in the Young Adult Book category versus 136 picture books; submissions mainly from UAE (115), Egypt (44), Lebanon (33), Jordan (31), Saudi Arabia (19).
YA prize AED 180,000 split between author and publisher; YA shortlist (Budjana; Mariam's Earring; Smile so I Can Be Stronger) contains no identifiable mystery title.
athar_applications: Quantifies the thin supply of Arabic YA books relative to picture books — consistent with a YA content gap ATHAR can fill; also a recognition channel (award) for ATHAR-commissioned YA case novellas.
limitations: Submissions ≠ market output; single year; genre of shortlisted titles not stated.
